p.src: The Classical Pattern: State and Update

u.src: The Classical Pattern: State and Update
en: The Classical Pattern: State and Update

p.src: Begin with a closed system, at least temporarily isolated from everything else. The word system is primitive here: it means the object whose history we want to predict. A state is everything that must be known at one instant in order to make that prediction. Classical mechanics supplies a law that updates one state into the next.

p.src:
For the simplest abstract coin, $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{coin}}=\{H,T\}.$ One possible law says that nothing happens: $H\longmapsto H,
  \qquad
  T\longmapsto T.$ Another law alternates the two states: $H\longmapsto T,
  \qquad
  T\longmapsto H.$ These examples are elementary, but they expose the architecture of a classical theory: $s(t)\longmapsto s(t+\Delta t).$ Once $s(t)$ is known, the update is deterministic.

p.src: The same pattern survives when the state space is continuous. A particle moving on a line requires both its position and momentum, $s=(q,p),$ so its state space is the phase plane. The number of possible states has become infinite, and the equations may be written in the elegant language of Lagrangians, Hamiltonians, and Poisson brackets, but the underlying idea has not changed. The state at one time contains what is needed to predict the state at another.

p.src: Abstraction Before Visualization

u.src: Abstraction Before Visualization
en: Abstraction Before Visualization

p.src: Classical motion is comparatively easy to picture because its concepts are drawn from ordinary experience. That advantage disappears when the relevant objects are too small, the velocities too large, or the dimension of the state space too high. No one literally visualizes the motion of an electron, four-dimensional spacetime, or a ten-dimensional space. This is not a deficiency peculiar to beginners. Human visual intuition was built for the everyday three-dimensional world.

A one-dimensional line is pictured as a mark in a plane. The picture quietly imports the ambient space in which our visual system knows how to operate.

p.src: The remedy is not to force a classical picture onto unfamiliar physics. It is to learn the abstract structure and let a new intuition grow from correct manipulations. Three-dimensional coordinates $(x,y,z)$ become four-dimensional coordinates $(x,y,z,w)$ by adding a symbol and extending the rules, not by acquiring a new organ of sight. Quantum mechanics demands the same discipline. Treating it as a strange mechanical model of little classical objects will repeatedly produce the wrong answer.

p.src: Classical State Spaces and Classical Logic

u.src: Classical State Spaces and Classical Logic
en: Classical State Spaces and Classical Logic

p.src:
A proposition about the system selects a subset of those possibilities. For the die, let $\begin{aligned}
  P_{\mathrm{odd}}&=\{1,3,5\},\\
  P_{\leq 3}&=\{1,2,3\}.\end{aligned}$ The statement odd and no greater than three corresponds to their intersection: $P_{\mathrm{odd}}\cap P_{\leq 3}=\{1,3\}.$ The inclusive statement odd or no greater than three corresponds to their union: $P_{\mathrm{odd}}\cup P_{\leq 3}
  =
  \{1,2,3,5\}.$ Thus classical conjunction and disjunction have the set-theoretic form $P\wedge Q\longleftrightarrow P\cap Q,
  \qquad
  P\vee Q\longleftrightarrow P\cup Q.$ If the subsets do not overlap, no state makes both propositions true.

p.src: This logic is tied to the classical conception of state. Quantum mechanics replaces the set of classical alternatives by a different mathematical object: a vector space. Only in a suitable classical limit does the vector-space description behave approximately like a set of exclusive configurations. Before constructing that space, we need an experiment that makes the replacement unavoidable.

p.src: The Simplest Quantum System

u.src: The Simplest Quantum System
en: The Simplest Quantum System

p.src:
The quantum analogue of the abstract coin is a two-outcome system called a qubit. Its measured alternatives may first be labeled heads and tails, but a numerical label is more useful: $\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}.$ Three notations will be used in parallel: $H\longleftrightarrow \sigma=+1\longleftrightarrow\uparrow,
  \qquad
  T\longleftrightarrow \sigma=-1\longleftrightarrow\downarrow.$ At first the arrows are only names. No ordinary geometric vector has yet been assumed.

p.src: The details of the detector are deliberately postponed. A good detector is defined operationally by the reliable relation between the system and its record. The observer need not be watching when the interaction occurs; the apparatus can record the result and be read later.

p.src:
Suppose the display reports $+1$. Reset the apparatus to its blank condition and repeat the same measurement immediately, before any independent evolution has time to act. A faithful detector reports $+1$ again. If the first result is $-1$, immediate repetitions likewise continue to report $-1$: $\begin{aligned}
  +1&\longrightarrow +1\longrightarrow +1\longrightarrow\cdots,\\
  -1&\longrightarrow -1\longrightarrow -1\longrightarrow\cdots.
\end{aligned}$ The first measurement can therefore be regarded as a preparation. It leaves the qubit in a state for which an immediate repetition of the same measurement has a definite result.

p.src: Turn the detector by $90^\circ$. If the prepared qubit were an ordinary upward pointer, its component along the horizontal detector axis would be zero: $\hat{\mathbf x}\cdot\hat{\mathbf z}=0.$ The quantum apparatus never reports zero. Every individual trial reports either $+1$ or $-1$.

p.src: Prepare a large collection of qubits with the upright apparatus, retaining those for which the result is $+1$. Measure each retained qubit once with the sideways apparatus. Half the trials give $+1$, half give $-1$, and the ensemble average is zero: $\expect{\sigma}_{\pi/2}=0.$ The average resembles the vanishing horizontal component of a classical pointer, but the individual records do not. The classical value $0$ has been replaced by a statistical balance between two discrete outcomes.

p.src:
In symbols, where $M_z$ and $M_x$ denote measurements along the two axes, $\begin{aligned}
  M_z&:+1,\\
  M_x&:\pm1,\\
  M_x&:\text{same result},\\
  M_z&:\pm1.
\end{aligned}$ The intermediate $x$-measurement has not merely uncovered a horizontal component while preserving the original vertical state. It has prepared a new state, and the original vertical definiteness is gone.

p.src: An Arbitrarily Rotated Analyzer

u.src: An Arbitrarily Rotated Analyzer
en: An Arbitrarily Rotated Analyzer

p.src:
Let the detector axis make an angle $\theta$ with the axis along which the ensemble was prepared. Every trial still yields $\sigma=\pm1.$ The relative frequencies vary with the angle so that the mean is $\expect{\sigma}_{\theta}=\cos\theta.$ The limiting cases are $\begin{aligned}
  \expect{\sigma}_{0}&=+1,\\
  \expect{\sigma}_{\pi/2}&=0,\\
  \expect{\sigma}_{\pi}&=-1.\end{aligned}$ Near $\theta=0$, most outcomes are $+1$, with an occasional $-1$. Near $\theta=\pi$, most are $-1$, with an occasional $+1$.

p.src: Pointers and Abstract Vectors

u.src: Pointers and Abstract Vectors
en: Pointers and Abstract Vectors

p.src: The experimental facts are now separated from the mathematics for a while. An ordinary arrow in physical space will be called a pointer. A mathematical vector is more general: it is an element of a vector space and need not point anywhere in ordinary space.

u.src: The experimental facts are now separated from the mathematics for a while. An ordinary arrow in physical space will be called a pointer. A mathematical vector is more general: it is an element of a vector space and need not point anywhere in ordinary space.
en: The experimental facts are now separated from the mathematics for a while. An ordinary arrow in physical space will be called a pointer. A mathematical vector is more general: it is an element of a vector space and need not point anywhere in ordinary space.

p.src:
A complex vector space $V$ is a collection of vectors for which vector addition and multiplication by complex scalars are defined and satisfy the usual linearity rules. In particular, for $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb C$, $\begin{aligned}
  u+v&=v+u,\\
  (u+v)+w&=u+(v+w),\\
  a(u+v)&=au+av,\\
  (a+b)u&=au+bu,\\
  (ab)u&=a(bu),\\
  1u&=u.\end{aligned}$ There is a zero vector $0$ and an additive inverse $-u$ for every $u$.

p.src:
The classroom discussion initially emphasizes only the operations and closure: $\begin{aligned}
  u,v\in V&\Longrightarrow u+v\in V,\\
  a\in\mathbb C,\ u\in V&\Longrightarrow au\in V.
\end{aligned}$ The zero vector and commutativity are then supplied in response to questions. The remaining familiar axioms state explicitly what is already used when the concrete column-vector model is introduced.

p.src:
Real numbers form a one-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb R$. Complex numbers form a one-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb C$, and a two-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb R$. Complex-valued functions $\psi(x)$ also form a complex vector space because $(\psi+\phi)(x)=\psi(x)+\phi(x),
  \qquad
  (z\psi)(x)=z\psi(x).$ This function-space example will later become central, but finite columns make the structure easier to see first.

u.src:

  \qquad
  (z\psi)(x)=z\psi(x).$ This function-space example will later become central, but finite columns make the structure easier to see first.

p.src: Norm and Positivity

u.src: Norm and Positivity
en: Norm and Positivity

p.src:
Set $\beta=\alpha$ in Equation : $\braket{\alpha}{\alpha}
  =
  \alpha_1^*\alpha_1+\alpha_2^*\alpha_2
  =
  |\alpha_1|^2+|\alpha_2|^2.$ This number equals its own complex conjugate, so it is real. It is nonnegative, and it vanishes only for the zero vector. The length is defined by $\|\alpha\|
  =
  \sqrt{\braket{\alpha}{\alpha}}.$ Complex components therefore produce an ordinary nonnegative real length.

  =

    1
  \end{pmatrix},
  \qquad

p.src:
The dimension can be characterized as the largest number of mutually orthogonal nonzero vectors. In a two-dimensional space there can be two such vectors but no third. To see this concretely, let $\ket{v}
  =
  \begin{pmatrix}
    v_1\\
    v_2
  \end{pmatrix}$ be orthogonal to both vectors in Equation . Then $\braket{e_1}{v}=v_1=0,
  \qquad
  \braket{e_2}{v}=v_2=0,$ so $\ket{v}=\ket{0}$. There is no third nonzero vector orthogonal to both.
